deep.reconstruction:
The page holds three independent research notes, likely from Hilbert's early notebook period, c. 1885-1890 (my inference). None is a worked derivation; each is a sketched programme.

(1) INVARIANTS OF ONE INTEGRAL LINEAR TRANSFORMATION.
Problem: let T in GL_n(Z) act on Z[x_1..x_n] by f(x) -> f(Tx). Find all integral polynomials f with f(Tx) = f(x), i.e. the invariant ring Z[x]^<T>.

Method: bring T to canonical form by the Fuchs-Hamburger canonisation, which is Jordan normal form over an algebraic extension. Hamburger (1873) gave it for the monodromy substitution of Fuchsian linear ODEs; Weierstrass, Jordan and Frobenius gave equivalent versions. T then splits into Jordan blocks J_k(lambda).

Reduction (Hilbert's claim, with my fill-in):
- The unipotent part of a block of size k acts on k coordinates x_0..x_{k-1} exactly as a unipotent element of SL_2 acts on the coefficients of a binary form of degree k-1.
- Polynomials invariant under a unipotent matrix u are, in characteristic 0, the invariants of its Zariski closure G_a.
- By Roberts' theorem (1861; Cayley's seminvariants), G_a-invariants on a sum of such blocks correspond to covariants, i.e. simultaneous invariants of the system of binary forms together with a linear form.
- So the problem 'leads to the setting-up of simultaneous binary invariants'.
- The semisimple (eigenvalue) part is a diagonalisable group. Its invariants are spanned by monomials whose exponents satisfy multiplicative relations among the eigenvalues; they are finitely generated by Gordan's lemma (my fill-in).
- Hence 'the finiteness of those invariants also follows', from Gordan's theorem for binary systems (1868).

Modern form: for a single linear transformation, the invariant ring is finitely generated. Proof: embed the unipotent part in an SL_2-action (Jacobson-Morozov), apply the Roberts-Weitzenboeck correspondence, then use finiteness for SL_2 (Gordan/Hilbert). This is precisely the standard proof of Weitzenboeck's theorem (1932).

Smallest examples (mine):
- J_2 = [[1,1],[0,1]], acting by (x,y) -> (x+y, y), has invariant ring C[y].
- J_3, acting by x0 -> x0+x1, x1 -> x1+x2, x2 -> x2, has invariants x2 and x1^2 - 2*x0*x2 - x1*x2. The latter is the analogue of the discriminant of a binary quadratic.

(2) EVERY ALGEBRAIC SYSTEM REDUCES TO QUADRATIC EQUATIONS.
Given polynomial equations F_j(x_1..x_m) = 0 of any degree, introduce a new unknown for every power and product, e.g. u = x^2, w = x*y, and so on. Each equation becomes linear in the new variables. Each defining relation (u - x^2 = 0, w - x*y = 0, u2 - x*u = 0, ...) is quadratic.

Example (mine): x^3 + y^3 - 1 = 0 becomes the system x*u + y*v - 1 = 0, u - x^2 = 0, v - y^2 = 0.

The new variety projects isomorphically onto the old one (it is the graph of a polynomial map). Hence every algebraic variety is isomorphic to an intersection of quadrics in a larger space ('all algebraic Gebilde can be generated by quadratic surfaces').

Hilbert concludes programmatically that one need only study the degenerations (Ausartungen) of systems of quadratic forms in order to 'have' all algebraic surfaces.

(3) CONTINUED FRACTIONS VIA DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS.
A sum or infinite series is approximated by an integral (Euler-Maclaurin, integral comparison). By analogy, Hilbert proposes to express infinite continued fractions, higher continued-fraction algorithms (Jacobi-Perron type) and other recursive structures through solutions of differential equations. This is a research suggestion, not a derivation.

Classical instance (mine): Lambert's/Gauss's continued fraction for tan x, or ratios of contiguous hypergeometric functions, solves a Riccati equation y' = 1 + y^2.
errors: (1) Integrality: Jordan form needs the eigenvalues, i.e. an algebraic extension of Q. The reduction directly gives invariants over C, or over Q after Galois descent. Finite generation over Z of Z[x]^T needs an extra argument the note does not give.

(1) The reduction to binary invariants covers the unipotent part. The interaction between blocks through multiplicative relations among eigenvalues (the torus part) must be handled separately, e.g. by Gordan's lemma. This is not mentioned, but the claim stays correct.

(1) A subtle step is implicit: polynomial invariants of a unipotent matrix (infinite cyclic group) coincide with invariants of the one-parameter group G_a. This is true in characteristic 0 but unproved in the note.

(2) The reduction itself is correct. The conclusion 'one only needs to study degenerations of systems of quadratic forms' is an overreach. Only pencils of quadrics (Weierstrass-Kronecker) have a tractable classification; general linear systems of quadrics are as complicated as all varieties, so nothing is simplified.

(2) The reduction gives a variety isomorphic to the original (via projection), not the original itself. Projectively one must also homogenise. 'Erzeugt' should be read as 'up to isomorphism/projection'.
(3) This is only a heuristic programme; no precise claim is made.

results.what: Invariants of a single linear transformation reduce, via Jordan canonical form, to simultaneous binary invariants/covariants; finiteness follows from Gordan's binary finiteness theorem
results.modern_name: Weitzenboeck's theorem (finite generation of invariants of a linear G_a-action), proved via the Roberts isomorphism/Jacobson-Morozov embedding into SL_2
results.usually_credited_to: R. Weitzenboeck (1932); ingredients from Roberts (1861), Cayley (seminvariants), Gordan (1868); modern proofs by Seshadri (1962) and Tyc (1998)

results.what: Canonical form of a linear substitution (Fuchs-Hamburger canonisation)

Every system of polynomial equations is equivalent (by introducing new variables for powers/products) to a system of quadratic equations; every algebraic variety is isomorphic to an intersection of quadrics
results.modern_name: Degree reduction to quadrics; the strong form (projective varieties cut out by quadrics after Veronese re-embedding) is Mumford's theorem
results.usually_credited_to: Folklore for the elementary form; Mumford (1970) for the projective statement

results.what: Programme: express infinite continued fractions and higher continued-fraction algorithms through solutions of differential equations, by analogy with series vs integrals
results.modern_name: Continued fractions and Riccati/hypergeometric ODEs; continuum limits of recurrences
results.usually_credited_to: Euler, Lambert, Gauss (hypergeometric continued fractions), Laguerre, Stieltjes

deep.surprise_reason: Note (1) is a correct sketch of the now-standard strategy behind Weitzenboeck's 1932 theorem. That strategy is: Jordan form, then unipotent block as binary form, then simultaneous binary invariants, then Gordan finiteness. It appears decades earlier in Hilbert's private notebook. It is only a programmatic remark without proof, and it fits Hilbert's known invariant-theory work and the classical Cayley/Roberts seminvariant theory. So it is a notable unpublished detail rather than a major priority claim. Notes (2) and (3) are folklore-level ideas or research wishes.

checkable.asserts: y is invariant under the 2x2 unipotent Jordan block (x,y)->(x+y,y).
x1^2-2*x0*x2-x1*x2 is a quadratic invariant of the 3x3 unipotent Jordan block (analogue of the binary quadratic discriminant).

checkable.asserts: Eliminating u,v from the quadratic system x*u+y*v-1, u-x^2, v-y^2 recovers the cubic x^3+y^3-1 (the elimination ideal in x,y is generated by it).
Lambert's continued fraction convergent for tan x (a solution of the Riccati ODE y'=1+y^2) agrees with tan x through order x^14.

transcription_corrections: 'Frob.[?]-Hamburgerschen' is more likely 'Fuchs-Hamburgerschen'. The handwriting reads 'Fuchs-Hamburgerschen', and Hamburger's 1873 canonical form of the fundamental substitution of Fuchsian linear ODEs is the natural reference.

The opening symbol 'A[?]' and the symbol in 'auf A[?] simultane quadratische Gl.' are the same abbreviation sign. In the second occurrence it must stand for a word like 'lauter' or a number ('N' simultaneous equations), so it is not a section letter 'A'. The reading remains uncertain.
'Alle Gleichung' should read 'Alle Gleichungen' (Hilbert's abbreviated plural).
In the last line of note 2, '[-...-]at[?]' is a struck-out word followed by 'at'; the line reads 'Dann hat man [struck] alle algebr. Flächen'.
'alle ganzen ganzzahligen Funktion' should read 'alle ganzen ganzzahligen Funktionen'.
'angenähert' and 'ausgedrückt' are confirmed; 'unendliche' in parentheses after 'Kettenbrüche' is confirmed.
